subject: History
board: National Curriculum KS3 (History is not offered at KS4)
source: National Curriculum KS3 (the development of Church, state and society in medieval Britain, 1066-1509); no school Drive history material for this unit, written from scratch | Spring 1 2027 (lessons 5 to 9): Tarbiyyah Secondary History Curriculum Intent; Hodder Understanding History KS3 scheme of work, Unit 2 (2.4A to 2.4C); Salahuddin and source enquiry from the intent

lessons.title: 1066: who should be king?
objectives: Explain why England had a succession crisis in January 1066
Compare the claims of Harold Godwinson, William of Normandy and Harald Hardrada

keywords.def: who takes over as ruler after a king dies
a person who says they have the right to something
a powerful nobleman who governed a large area
the council of nobles who advised the Anglo-Saxon king
the person who inherits a title or property

starter: Who was Alfred the Great and what did he achieve?
Why do countries need rules for who becomes ruler?

teach.heading: Bismillah: a country without a clear heir
bullets: Edward the Confessor died on 5 January 1066
At least three men wanted the throne
teach.note: Begin with bismillah and a brief note on fairness and justice in leadership. Ask pupils: if a leader dies with no children, who should rule? Collect fair rules, then compare with 1066.

teach.heading: Harold Godwinson
bullets: Harold was England's most powerful earl
He claimed Edward named him heir on his deathbed
The witan chose him as king
teach.note: Harold was crowned on 6 January 1066. Ask: is being chosen by the witan a strong claim? He was also Edward's brother-in-law. The Bayeux Tapestry later told the story from the Norman side, so treat it as biased.

teach.heading: William of Normandy
bullets: He said Edward promised him the throne
He said Harold swore an oath to support him
teach.note: Norman sources claim Harold swore an oath to William in 1064. Historians cannot confirm all details. Ask pupils how we judge claims when there are no neutral sources.

teach.heading: Harald Hardrada
bullets: He claimed the throne through an earlier deal
He had a fierce reputation as a warrior
teach.note: Hardrada's claim came from an agreement between a previous Norwegian king and a previous English king, Harthacnut. Support came from Tostig, Harold's exiled brother.

practice: Give one reason why Harold had a good claim.
Why might William's claim be seen as weak?
independent: Complete a table comparing the three claimants: relationship to Edward, support, strengths, weaknesses
Rank their claims from strongest to weakest and explain your choice
Write a paragraph beginning 'The most convincing claimant was ... because ...'
exit: Which claimant was chosen by the witan?
lessons.homework: Write 5 sentences explaining why England had a crisis in 1066.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: table with partial answers and word bank. Stretch: judge whether a claim by blood or a claim by choice was fairer.

lessons.title: Stamford Bridge and Hastings: why did William win?
objectives: Narrate the main events of September to October 1066
Evaluate the reasons why William won the Battle of Hastings

keywords.def: the battle on 25 September 1066 where Harold defeated Hardrada
the battle on 14 October 1066 where William defeated Harold
soldiers who fight on horseback
a tight line of soldiers with overlapping shields
a soldier who fires arrows with a bow

starter: Name the three claimants to the throne in 1066.

teach.heading: Two invasions
bullets: Hardrada landed in the north in September
William waited in Normandy for a south wind
Harold had to face both threats
teach.note: Harold's army waited for William on the south coast all summer, then went home to harvest. Ask: what problems did Harold face with defence and supplies?

teach.heading: Stamford Bridge, 25 September
bullets: Harold marched about 185 miles north in days
He surprised and destroyed Hardrada's army
teach.note: A great victory, but his army was exhausted. Three days later William landed at Pevensey on 28 September. Ask pupils what Harold should do next.

teach.heading: Hastings, 14 October
bullets: Harold's army held a ridge in a shield wall
Norman knights pretended to retreat, drawing Saxons out
teach.note: Historians still debate if the feigned retreat was real. Harold was killed, traditionally by an arrow to the eye, though that is debated. Show the Bayeux Tapestry and discuss reliability.

teach.heading: Why did William win?
bullets: Harold's army was tired from the march
Norman cavalry and archers were strong
Harold's death left his army leaderless
teach.note: Build a causation diagram: luck (wind, Harold's march), leadership (William's tactics), and Harold's mistakes. Encourage pupils to rank causes and justify: this is the skill for GCSE.

practice: Where was Harold when William landed?
Name two reasons why William won.
independent: Produce a timeline of September-October 1066 with six events
Rank the reasons for William's victory in order of importance
Write an explanation: 'William won the Battle of Hastings because ...' using two causes
exit: On what date was the Battle of Hastings?
Give one cause of Harold's defeat.
lessons.homework: Draw a plan of the Battle of Hastings with labels for both sides.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: pre-written timeline cards to order. Stretch: argue whether luck or skill was more important.

lessons.title: How did the Normans control England?
objectives: Describe how William used castles, land and law to control England
Explain the Harrying of the North and the Domesday Book

keywords.def: a castle with a mound (motte) and a walled yard (bailey)
a system where land was given in return for loyalty and service
William's 1086 survey of land and wealth in England
an uprising against those in power
a powerful Norman lord who held land from the king

starter: Why did William win at Hastings? Give two reasons.
On which date was Hastings fought?
Why might some English people not accept William as king?

teach.heading: Castles
bullets: Normans built motte and bailey castles
Early castles were built of wood quickly
Later castles were rebuilt in stone
teach.note: Show a diagram of a motte and bailey. Ask what message a castle sent to the local English. The Tower of London's White Tower was begun in the 1070s.

teach.heading: The feudal system
bullets: The king owned all the land
Barons held land in return for knights
Peasants worked the land for the lord
teach.note: Draw a pyramid: king, barons, knights, peasants. Most English lords lost their land to Normans. Ask: how did this keep the king safe from rivals?

teach.heading: The Harrying of the North
bullets: William's army destroyed crops and villages
teach.note: This was a brutal event, also recorded in the Domesday Book which shows many places as 'waste'. Ask whether it was necessary. Discuss with sensitivity: Islam teaches us to oppose oppression and to be just.

teach.heading: The Domesday Book
bullets: Recorded who owned land, animals and people
teach.note: The name comes from 'doomsday', meaning final judgement, because its decisions couldn't be appealed. Ask: what would a government do with this information? What are the modern equivalents?

practice: Why were castles built so quickly?
Who owned all the land in the feudal system?
What was the Domesday Book for?
independent: Draw and label a motte and bailey castle
Create a feudal pyramid with a sentence about each level
Answer: How far did William use fear to control England? Use two examples
exit: Name one way William controlled England.
What year was the Domesday Book made?
lessons.homework: Use the Open Domesday website or a library source to find one place in the Domesday Book near London and record what it says.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: castle labelling diagram with word bank. Stretch: compare control by fear with control by law and fairness.

lessons.title: Magna Carta and limiting the power of the king
objectives: Explain why the barons rebelled against King John
Describe the main ideas in Magna Carta of 1215

keywords.def: the Great Charter that limited the king's power in 1215
money collected by a ruler or government
a written document that grants rights
fair treatment under the law

starter: Why do rulers need to be fair?

teach.heading: King John
bullets: He demanded high taxes to pay for war
teach.note: John lost Normandy in 1204. Ask pupils how people react when taxes go up but a king is losing wars. Begin with bismillah and note that Islam teaches rulers are accountable for how they treat their people.

teach.heading: Rebellion of the barons
bullets: John argued with the Pope and the barons
He imprisoned people without fair trials
Barons rebelled in 1215 and took London
teach.note: Explain it in layers: money, justice, loyalty. The barons were mainly protecting their own interests, not fairness for everyone.

teach.heading: Magna Carta, June 1215
bullets: The king must obey the law
No free man to be punished without lawful judgement
teach.note: Sealed 15 June 1215. Clauses 39 and 40 are most famous. Misconception: Magna Carta gave rights to everyone; it applied mainly to free men.

teach.heading: What happened next?
bullets: It was reissued after John died in 1216
teach.note: Magna Carta failed at first. It was reissued in 1216, 1217 and 1225. Its importance is its idea that even the king is under the law, which influenced later ideas about rights. Compare with Islamic principles of justice carefully.

practice: Why were the barons unhappy with John?
What did the barons force the king to agree?
Was Magna Carta a success in 1215? Give a reason.
independent: Create a cause-and-consequence chart for Magna Carta
Explain in a paragraph why Magna Carta is still remembered today
Write: 'The most important clause was ... because ...'
exit: Where was Magna Carta sealed and in which year?
Name one thing Magna Carta said the king could not do.
lessons.homework: Find out one modern right in Britain linked to the idea of fair trial and write 3 sentences about it.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: simplified version of clauses with vocabulary support. Stretch: evaluate whether Magna Carta mattered more in 1215 or later.

lessons.title: Historians, Christendom and the Islamic world in 1095
lessons.bigQuestion: What did the world around Jerusalem look like in 1095?
objectives: To understand how historians think and what Christendom and the Islamic world were like in 1095
successCriteria: All: name the six concepts historians use
Most: describe the main powers in Christendom and the Islamic world in 1095
Some: explain why Jerusalem mattered to Muslims, Christians and Jews
lessons.smsc: Cultural: why one city is sacred to three faiths

keywords.def: the Christian lands of Europe in the Middle Ages
a state ruled by a caliph, a successor to the Prophet as leader of Muslims
the eastern Christian empire ruled from Constantinople
Turkish Muslim rulers who took power in much of the Middle East in the 1000s
the order in which events happened

hook.text: Why might three faiths all care so much about one city?

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'Exalted is He who took His servant by night from al-Masjid al-Haram to al-Masjid al-Aqsa, whose surroundings We have blessed' (al-Isra 17:1). Al-Aqsa was the first qiblah of the Muslims. This is why Jerusalem (al-Quds) is so precious to Muslims.

starter.q: Which came first: the Norman Conquest or Magna Carta?
In which century is the year 1095?
Name the city where the Abbasid caliphs lived.

teach.heading: What historians do
bullets: Similarity and difference, significance, sources and interpretations
teach.note: These six concepts are the questions we ask in every unit.

teach.heading: Christendom in 1095
bullets: Latin West: led spiritually by the Pope in Rome
The Byzantines had lost land to the Seljuks
teach.note: The Seljuks beat the Byzantine army at Manzikert in 1071 and took much of Anatolia.

teach.heading: The Islamic world in 1095
bullets: Abbasid caliph in Baghdad, with Seljuk sultans holding real power
teach.note: The Muslim world was rich in learning and trade, but politically divided: this matters for the Crusades.

teach.heading: Jerusalem
bullets: Holy to Muslims: al-Aqsa and the Night Journey
teach.note: Caliph Umar ibn al-Khattab received the city peacefully. Christians and Jews lived and worshipped there under Muslim rule.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share results.

check.q: In 1095, who held real power in Baghdad?
check.why: The Abbasid caliph was in Baghdad, but Seljuk sultans held the real power. The Pope and emperor ruled in Christendom.

practice.q: Which historical concept is about the order of events?
practice.model:
Read the toolkit.
Order of events = chronology.
So the answer is chronology.

practice.q: Why did the Byzantine emperor need help in 1095?
practice.a: The Seljuk Turks had taken much of his land after Manzikert in 1071

practice.q: Why is Jerusalem holy to Muslims?
practice.a: Al-Aqsa Mosque is there; it was the first qiblah and linked to the Night Journey

independent.q: Core: Label the map: Rome, Constantinople, Baghdad, Cairo, Jerusalem; shade Christendom and the Islamic world.
independent.a: Correctly placed cities; Western and Byzantine Christendom shaded; Seljuk and Fatimid lands shaded
independent.model: Teacher shows it first: Constantinople on the strait between Europe and Asia; label it 'Byzantine capital'.

independent.q: Extend: In the portal response box, write a paragraph describing the Islamic world in 1095. Start: 'In 1095 the Islamic world was ...'
independent.a: For example: rich in learning and trade but divided between the Abbasids, the Seljuks and the Fatimids

independent.q: Stretch: Why might divisions in the Islamic world matter if an army attacked?
independent.a: Divided rulers might not unite to defend their lands

exit.q: Jerusalem had been under Muslim rule since:
Big question: what did the world around Jerusalem look like in 1095?
exit.a: Christendom split between the Pope's West and the Byzantine East; the Islamic world rich but divided between Seljuks and Fatimids; Jerusalem holy to all three faiths

lessons.homework: Read Hodder Understanding History KS3 lesson 2.4A introduction (or the portal summary) and note three reasons Jerusalem mattered.
lessons.send: SEND: map with cities pre-dotted and a word bank. EAL: glossary of caliph, pope, emperor, sultan. Stretch: research the Battle of Manzikert, 1071.
resources: Understanding History: Key Stage 3 (Hodder, 2019) scheme of work, Unit 2 (introduction to 2.4)
Map of the Mediterranean and Middle East in 1095 to 1192 (portal printable)
Historian's toolkit card: the six concepts (portal printable)

lessons.title: How can we explain the First Crusade?
lessons.bigQuestion: Why would thousands of people walk 3,000 km to fight?
objectives: To understand the causes of the First Crusade and the motives of those who joined
successCriteria: All: say what the Pope asked for in 1095
Most: explain three different motives for joining
Some: judge which motive was most important, with evidence
lessons.smsc: Moral: what makes a war just or unjust

keywords.def: a war that the Pope declared to be holy
a journey to a holy place
a reason for doing something
a reason an event happened
the Pope who called the First Crusade in 1095

hook.text: What would make you leave your home and family for years?

islamicLink.text: Islam has clear rules for war: the Prophet, peace be upon him, forbade the killing of women and children (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim). Allah also says: 'Fight in the way of Allah those who fight you, but do not transgress' (al-Baqarah 2:190). Muslims judge every war, including their own, by these rules.

starter.q: Jerusalem was under Muslim rule from:
Who beat the Byzantines at Manzikert in 1071?

teach.heading: The call, 1095
bullets: Byzantine emperor Alexios asked the Pope for soldiers
Pope Urban II spoke at Clermont, France
He called for an armed pilgrimage to Jerusalem
teach.note: The Council of Clermont was in November 1095. The Pope promised forgiveness of sins to those who went.

teach.heading: Who went?
teach.note: A 'People's Crusade' of poorly armed people set off first in 1096 and was largely destroyed in Anatolia.

teach.heading: Why did they go?
teach.note: Pupils give the letter and column.

teach.heading: What did the Pope want?
bullets: To stop knights fighting each other in Europe
teach.note: Ask: was the Pope's motive only religious?

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share results.

check.why: Alexios asked for help; Pope Urban II made the call at Clermont. Salahuddin lived a century later.

practice.q: Write a PEEL point about religious motives.
practice.a: Point: many crusaders were driven by religion. Evidence: the Pope promised forgiveness of sins. Explain: so they believed going would save their souls. Link: so religion was a key cause.
practice.model:
Point: Many crusaders went for religious reasons.
Evidence: Urban II promised forgiveness of sins.
Explain: they believed this would save them from punishment after death.
Link: so religion explains why so many joined.

practice.a: For example: land, riches or fame

practice.q: Why did the Byzantine emperor want help?
practice.a: To win back land lost to the Seljuks

independent.q: Core: Write a PEEL paragraph in the portal response box: 'The most important reason people joined the First Crusade was ...'
independent.a: A clear point, evidence (forgiveness, land, adventure), explanation and link back to the question
independent.model: Teacher goes through it first: 'The most important reason was religion (P). The Pope promised forgiveness of sins (E). For people who feared punishment in the hereafter, this was powerful (E). So religion explains why even the poor joined (L).'

independent.q: Extend: Add a sentence on a second motive and why it is less important.
independent.a: For example: Some wanted land, but most knights spent their own money and many returned home poorer

independent.q: Stretch: Was the Pope's motive the same as the crusaders'? Explain.
independent.a: Partly: he wanted to help Byzantium and strengthen his own power, while many crusaders sought forgiveness or land

exit.q: The Pope called the crusade at:
Big question: why would thousands of people walk 3,000 km to fight?
exit.a: Religious belief (forgiveness, pilgrimage), hope of land and riches, adventure and status, and the Pope's call

lessons.homework: Complete Hodder Worksheet 2.4A.1 (motives) or the portal version.
lessons.send: SEND: motive cards with pictures; PEEL frame with sentence starters. EAL: glossary for crusade, pilgrimage, motive. Stretch: compare motives of knights and the poor.

lessons.title: The journey and the capture of Jerusalem, 1099
lessons.bigQuestion: Why do accounts of the capture of Jerusalem disagree?
objectives: To understand how the crusaders reached and captured Jerusalem and how historians interpret the violence
successCriteria: All: order the main events of the journey to Jerusalem
Most: describe the challenges crusaders faced
Some: compare interpretations of the massacre in 1099
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: the route across Anatolia and Syria
lessons.smsc: Moral: fairness when telling a painful history

keywords.def: surrounding a place to force it to surrender
a tall wooden tower pushed against city walls
the killing of many people who cannot defend themselves
a view of the past made by someone later
a land ruled by crusaders after 1099

hook.text: A city is captured after a long siege. Who decides how the story is told?

islamicLink.text: Allah commands justice even towards enemies: 'Do not let hatred of a people lead you to be unjust. Be just: that is nearer to righteousness' (al-Ma'idah 5:8). Historians, too, must be fair to all sides when they tell the story.

teach.heading: The journey
teach.note: Heat, hunger, disease and battle killed many crusaders on the way.

teach.heading: The challenges
teach.note: Muslim rulers did not unite against them; the Fatimids had only recently taken Jerusalem.

teach.heading: The siege of Jerusalem
bullets: Many Muslim and Jewish inhabitants were killed
teach.note: State facts calmly, with no graphic detail.

teach.heading: Interpretations
bullets: Crusader writers boasted of the killing
Ibn al-Athir, writing over 100 years later, gave a very high figure
teach.note: Modern historians think the number was lower than some sources claim, but agree it was a massacre.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share results.

check.q: When was Jerusalem captured by the crusaders?
check.why: 1095 was the call; 1187 was Salahuddin's recapture.

practice.q: Put in order: Antioch, Jerusalem, Constantinople, Nicaea.
practice.model:
They met first at Constantinople.
Then crossed to Nicaea.
Then Antioch.
Last, Jerusalem.

practice.q: Name two challenges on the journey.
Why might a crusader chronicler and a Muslim historian describe 1099 differently?
practice.a: Different sides, purposes and distance in time

independent.q: Core: Make an annotated map of the route to Jerusalem with five places and one challenge at each.
independent.a: Constantinople, Nicaea, Dorylaeum, Antioch, Jerusalem with challenges such as hunger, battle, heat
independent.model: Teacher shows it first: dot at Antioch, label 'long siege 1097 to 1098: hunger and disease'.

independent.q: Extend: In the portal response box, explain why the interpretations of 1099 differ.
independent.a: Writers were on different sides, wrote at different times and had different purposes, so they chose and exaggerated different details

independent.q: Stretch: What was set up after 1099?
independent.a: Crusader states: the Kingdom of Jerusalem, Antioch, Edessa and Tripoli

exit.a: Surrounding a place to force it to surrender
options: Surrounding a place to force it to surrender

exit.q: Big question: why do accounts of the capture of Jerusalem disagree?
exit.a: The writers were on different sides, wrote at different times and had different purposes

lessons.homework: Complete Hodder Worksheet 2.4C (interpretations of the siege) or the portal version.
lessons.send: SEND: route map with places pre-marked. EAL: siege, wall, tower, massacre. Stretch: read about the crusader states and where they were.

lessons.title: Salahuddin, Hattin and the Third Crusade
lessons.bigQuestion: Why is Salahuddin remembered with respect even by his enemies?
objectives: To understand how Salahuddin recaptured Jerusalem and how the Third Crusade ended
successCriteria: All: say when and how Salahuddin took Jerusalem
Some: explain why the Third Crusade ended in a truce
lessons.smsc: Moral: mercy and justice in victory

keywords.def: the Muslim leader who united Egypt and Syria and retook Jerusalem in 1187
the battle in 1187 where Salahuddin defeated the crusader army
an agreement to stop fighting for a time
money paid to free a prisoner
the crusade of 1189 to 1192 led partly by Richard I of England

hook.text: How should a winner treat the people of a city he has just taken?

islamicLink.text: When Salahuddin took Jerusalem in 1187, he did not take revenge for 1099. This followed the Prophet's example: when the Prophet, peace be upon him, conquered Makkah he forgave his enemies. Allah says: 'Let them pardon and overlook. Would you not love that Allah should forgive you?' (an-Nur 24:22).

starter.q: Jerusalem was captured by crusaders in:

starter.a: A view of the past made later
options: A view of the past made later

starter.a: Kingdom of Jerusalem, Antioch, Edessa or Tripoli
Surrounding a place to force it to surrender

teach.heading: Salahuddin (صلاح الدين)
bullets: Born in Tikrit, about 1137 or 1138, of Kurdish family
teach.note: Uniting Muslim lands was the key to his success: compare with the division of 1099.

teach.heading: Hattin and Jerusalem, 1187
bullets: 4 July 1187: crusader army defeated at Hattin
Most inhabitants allowed to leave on paying ransom
teach.note: Many who could not pay were freed. No massacre followed.

teach.heading: 1099 and 1187 compared
teach.note: Pupils add points in the chat.

points: people leave on ransom; many freed

teach.heading: The Third Crusade
bullets: Richard I of England and Philip II of France
teach.note: At Acre Richard had about 2,700 Muslim prisoners killed. In 1192 the Treaty of Jaffa made a three-year truce: Jerusalem stayed Muslim and Christian pilgrims could visit.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share results.

check.q: How did the Third Crusade end?
options: A truce: Jerusalem stayed Muslim and pilgrims could visit
check.why: The Treaty of Jaffa (1192) left Jerusalem under Muslim rule with access for Christian pilgrims.

practice.a: For example: in 1099 the inhabitants were massacred; in 1187 most were allowed to leave
practice.model:
Choose one feature: what happened to the people?
1099: massacre.
1187: allowed to leave on ransom, many freed.
So the treatment of people was very different.

practice.q: Why could Salahuddin win in 1187 when Muslims lost in 1099?
practice.a: He had united Egypt and Syria

practice.q: What did the Treaty of Jaffa agree?
practice.a: A three-year truce; Jerusalem stayed Muslim; Christian pilgrims could visit

independent.q: Core: In the portal response box, write two PEEL paragraphs: 'Salahuddin is remembered with respect because ...'
independent.a: Points on uniting Muslims, victory at Hattin, mercy in 1187, and honourable truce with Richard, each with evidence
independent.model: Teacher shows paragraph 1: 'Salahuddin is respected for his mercy (P). In 1187 most inhabitants were allowed to leave and many were freed (E). This contrasted with 1099 and followed Islamic rules of war (E). So even enemies respected him (L).'

independent.q: Extend: Was the Third Crusade a success for the crusaders? Explain.
independent.a: Partly: they took Acre and coastal towns, but failed to retake Jerusalem

independent.q: Stretch: Why might European writers later praise an enemy leader?
independent.a: His honourable conduct impressed them, and praising a strong enemy also made their own heroes look brave

exit.q: The Battle of Hattin was in:
Big question: why is Salahuddin remembered with respect even by his enemies?
exit.a: He united Muslims, won Jerusalem back, showed mercy in 1187 and made an honourable truce

lessons.homework: Make a fact file on Salahuddin with five dated events.
lessons.send: SEND: timeline cards and a PEEL frame. EAL: glossary: truce, ransom, mercy. Stretch: research the Battle of Arsuf (1191).

lessons.title: Source enquiry: how reliable are accounts of the Crusades? Unit quiz
lessons.bigQuestion: Can we trust anyone who wrote about the Crusades?
objectives: To understand how to judge the reliability of sources about the Crusades
successCriteria: All: identify who wrote a source, when and why
Most: explain how provenance affects reliability
Some: reach a balanced judgement using two sources
lessons.smsc: Moral: fairness and checking before we believe

keywords.def: who made a source, when and why
how far a source can be trusted
a one-sided view
a written record of events in time order
check one source against another

hook.text: If two people saw the same football match, why might they describe it differently?

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'O you who believe, if a wrongdoer brings you news, verify it' (al-Hujurat 49:6). Muslim scholars of hadith built careful methods to check every narrator. Historians ask the same questions of every source.

starter.q: The Battle of Hattin was in:
When was Jerusalem captured by crusaders?

teach.heading: Four writers
teach.note: All are real writers; we use paraphrased summaries of what they wrote.

teach.heading: Provenance questions
teach.note: NOP: Nature, Origin, Purpose.

teach.heading: Judging reliability
bullets: Written later: distant, but can compare
teach.note: Model with Ibn Shaddad's life of Salahuddin.

model.problem: How reliable is Ibn Shaddad on Salahuddin?
steps: Corroborate: crusader sources also report his mercy in 1187
model.answer: Reliable on events he saw; likely to praise; trusted more where other sources agree.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share results.

check.q: Which source on 1099 was written furthest from the event?
check.why: Ibn al-Athir wrote in the early 1200s, over a century later.

practice.q: What is the provenance of the Gesta Francorum?
practice.a: An anonymous crusader, about 1100, to record and celebrate the crusade
practice.model:
Nature: a chronicle.
Origin: an unknown crusader, about 1100.
Purpose: to record and celebrate.
So it is close to events but one-sided.

practice.q: Give one strength of an eyewitness source.

independent.q: Core: Unit quiz on the portal (12 questions: Christendom, motives, 1099, Salahuddin, the Third Crusade, sources).
independent.a: Answers in the portal quiz key
independent.model: Teacher does question 1 aloud: 'Who held real power in Baghdad in 1095?' The Seljuk sultans.

independent.q: Extend: In the portal response box: 'How reliable is the Gesta Francorum about 1099?' Use NOP.
independent.a: Close to events and an eyewitness, but written to celebrate the crusade, so likely to glorify the crusaders; useful when corroborated

independent.q: Stretch: Which source is most useful for the big question and why?
independent.a: Reasoned answer comparing provenance and corroboration
